rules.statement: Written sentences over 25 words are flagged.
rules.rationale: GOV.UK caps sentences at 25 words; NN/g suggests 15-20 even for experts. Authorities disagree, so this warns and never errors.

rules.statement: Spoken sentences over 16 words are flagged.
rules.rationale: CRS gives 8-16 words as the average spoken sentence and calls longer ones harder for listeners; using the top of that range as a per-sentence flag is this plugin's choice.

rules.statement: Reading grade is reported, never targeted.
rules.rationale: A randomised trial found no comprehension difference between grade 8 and grade 14 versions; rewriting to hit a score does not help readers.

rules.statement: Passive voice is counted and reported, not banned.
rules.rationale: AR 25-50 requires active voice, but a controlled study found active rewrites changed neither length nor comprehension. Use passive when the actor is unknown or irrelevant.

rules.statement: A three-word phrase repeated 3 or more times is flagged.
rules.rationale: Model-assisted writing repeats model-supplied phrases; the 3-occurrence threshold is this plugin's choice. Deliberate repetition in speeches is exempt by form.

rules.statement: Sentences opening with There is / There are are flagged.
rules.rationale: AR 25-50 asks writers to avoid opening with It is / There is / There are.

conflicts.note: Fix by deleting the empty opener, not by swapping in 'serves as' or 'boasts', which is a documented AI tell.

rules.statement: 'serves as', 'stands as', 'functions as' in place of is/are are flagged.
rules.rationale: LLM text often replaces simple is/are constructions; plain copulas read as human. A style finding, not an authorship verdict.

conflicts.note: Plain-language rules discourage empty 'There is' openers; prefer rewriting around a real subject and verb.

rules.statement: No leaked chatbot markup or unfilled placeholders.
rules.rationale: Citation markup such as oaicite or turn0search0 and utm_source=chatgpt.com links are unambiguous artifacts. Placeholders like [Your Name] are errors because they must not ship; a deliberate template should use a different placeholder form or fill them.

rules.statement: Bracketed placeholders are listed until filled.
rules.rationale: An honest [placeholder] beats an invented fact, but an unfilled one that ships is a documented artifact; list them so none ship.

rules.statement: Promotional words (groundbreaking, renowned, nestled, profound ...) are flagged in factual forms.
rules.rationale: Promotional tone and undue claims of significance are signs of generated text and weaken factual prose. A style finding, not an authorship verdict.

rules.statement: Three or more distinct era-tagged AI vocabulary terms in one draft are flagged.
rules.rationale: One or two such words may be coincidental; many together are a strong signal. The count of 3 is this plugin's choice. A style finding, not an authorship verdict.

rules.statement: Instructions avoid please, simply, it's easy, quickly and at this time.
rules.rationale: Google's style guide removes these: 'simply' and 'easy' blame the reader when a step is hard; 'please' and placeholders add length without meaning.

rules.statement: Spoken drafts report read-aloud time at the form's planning WPM.
rules.rationale: CRS plans ~130 wpm; TED talks run faster than lectures; individual speakers vary widely, so the figure is a planning estimate.

rules.statement: Scripts report estimated pages and runtime with a ±20% band.
rules.rationale: Follows suggests treating one page as about one minute, ±20%, since few scripts land close to the rule; multi-cam runs about twice the pages per minute because dialogue is double-spaced.

rules.statement: Every Fountain double-bracket note ([[ … ]]) is closed with ]].
rules.rationale: A [[ without its ]] (often after an editor strips the two-space line inside a note) turns note text into script text, which inflates page and word counts.

rules.statement: Every choice target, next pointer and start names an existing, unique node.
rules.rationale: A missing or duplicate target breaks the conversation at runtime.

rules.statement: Every node offers choices, a next node, or ends explicitly.
rules.rationale: ink treats loose ends as errors: the story 'ran out of content'.

rules.statement: Every node is reachable from the start node.
rules.rationale: Unreachable content is written but never seen, usually a broken link or a leftover. ink treats loose ends as errors; extending that to nodes nothing leads to is this plugin's check.

rules.statement: A choice set includes at least one unconditional choice.
rules.rationale: If every choice is gated, the player can be left with no options; ink uses fallback choices for this.

rules.statement: Each line fits the form's text box (default 40 characters × 2 lines).
rules.rationale: Accessibility guidelines cap subtitle lines at 40 characters and 2 lines; lines that overflow are split mid-thought or shrink.

rules.statement: Bark pools have more than one line and no near-repeats (word overlap ≥ 0.6).
rules.rationale: Salience systems rotate least-recently-used lines; a single-line or near-duplicate pool repeats audibly. The 0.6 overlap threshold is this plugin's choice.

rules.statement: Stop joking when a scene turns genuinely serious; a joke that stays should keep the pain visible.
rules.rationale: Jokes release tension; Espenson names three kinds that keep it: a coping joke that falls flat, bitter self-deprecation, and an attempt to appease.

rules.statement: Jokes grow from the scene's comic premise.
rules.rationale: A WGA West mentor advises that scenes are funnier when the scene has a comic premise and the jokes grow out of it.

rules.statement: The main result or request comes in the first or second sentence.
rules.rationale: The Army writing standard puts the bottom line up front; readers who stop early still get it.

rules.statement: Every claim is supported by the data given; missing values are [placeholders], never invented.
rules.rationale: Plugin policy: report only what the data given supports and mark missing values as [placeholders]; generated prose is documented to drift into promotional and puffed-up claims.

rules.statement: The first 30 seconds confirm the title and thumbnail promise, and the video delivers it.
rules.rationale: YouTube reads 30-second retention as whether the opening matched the packaging, and removes egregious clickbait whose promise the video never delivers.

rules.statement: A draft with a declared target lands within ±10% of it.
rules.rationale: Spoken length is planned from words at a rate (CRS) and script runtime from pages (±20% across 2,520 scripts, Follows); the ±10% tolerance is this plugin's choice. Report measured numbers; never assert compliance.

rules.statement: No timestamped segment runs faster than 180 words per minute.
rules.rationale: Broadcast subtitle timing assumes 160-180 wpm speech; narration packed faster than that will not fit its timestamps. Using the top of the range as the cap is this plugin's choice.

rules.statement: Multi-cam action and description are written in ALL CAPS.
rules.rationale: Multi-camera scripts write action and description in ALL CAPS, and run about twice the pages of a single-camera script for the same runtime.

rules.statement: Act markers (COLD OPEN, ACT, TAG, END OF ...) are centered >text<, not # sections.
rules.rationale: Fountain omits sections from formatted output, so a marker written as # disappears from the printed script.

rules.statement: A node the player can reach more than once has rotating variants.
rules.rationale: Repeat visits need variants or summaries; a hub that repeats one line on every visit makes an implausibly patient NPC. Nodes reached only through conditional links are not flagged, since the condition is taken to show the node once, so an always-true condition can hide a repeat.

rules.statement: From the start, an ending is reachable without depending on any condition.
rules.rationale: If every way out is gated, a player who fails the condition is trapped in the loop; ink's fallback choices exist to prevent running out of options.

rules.statement: Each step starts with an imperative verb, or a short location phrase and then the verb.
rules.rationale: Google and Microsoft agree: lead with the action (location first is allowed). Steps that open with 'You', 'The' or 'It' describe instead of instruct.

rules.statement: A procedure with one step is a bullet, not a numbered list.
rules.rationale: Google formats a single-step procedure as a bullet.

rules.statement: Every failure state says where to resume, and 'nothing happens' cases give a time limit or a check.
rules.rationale: Cutting information causes task failure; readers who hit an error need the way back in.

rules.statement: Each voiced speaker's measured style stays inside the voice bible's target ranges.
rules.rationale: Character voice is measurable; drift from a character's measured profile shows up as changed sentence length, contractions and exclamations. Ranges come from the project's own bible, and speakers with fewer than 40 words are not checked because their rates are noise.

rules.statement: Every voice bible in the project loads: valid YAML and schema, id matching the file name, unique ids, and each speaker claimed by one bible.
rules.rationale: A broken style guide cannot check anyone; fix the file so voice rules can run.

rules.statement: A speaker never uses a word their voice bible bans.
rules.rationale: Concrete character style guides name what a character would and would not say.

rules.statement: In a project with voice bibles, every speaker resolves to one.
rules.rationale: A speaker without a style guide cannot be checked or handed to translators and voice actors.

rules.statement: Swap test: no line could be given to another character without anyone noticing.
rules.rationale: Strong writers' characters are distinguishable by their speech; weak ones cluster.

rules.statement: The form fixes the line count: sonnet 14, villanelle 19, sestina 39, limerick 5, haiku 3, and ballad stanzas of 4.
rules.rationale: poets.org defines the sonnet as fourteen lines, the villanelle as five tercets and a quatrain (19), the sestina as six six-line stanzas and a three-line envoi (39), the limerick as five lines, the haiku as three lines and the ballad as quatrain stanzas. It says "traditionally" of the sonnet, and Sonnet or Not, Bot says fixed-form rules are "likely to be stretched or broken by poets" and that haiku can mean short poems with any number of lines, so this warns and never errors.

rules.statement: End rhymes follow the scheme, the form's or the one the draft declares in its frontmatter (a letter per line, x for an unconstrained line): each rhyme group matches its first line.
rules.rationale: poets.org gives the schemes: Shakespearean abab cdcd efef gg, Petrarchan abbaabba then cdecde or cdcdcd, limerick AABBA (the fifth line "either repeats the first line or rhymes with it", so a repeated word counts), ballad ABCB or ABAB, villanelle two rhymes. Each group is compared with its first line instead of comparing scheme letters, because one missed rhyme shifts every later letter. Rhyme is read from CMUdict, US English only, whose maintainers "expect a number of errors, omissions and inconsistencies"; the classes follow Prosodic's definitions and are conventions. A slant pair, an eye pair or a pair resting on a guessed or variant pronunciation is only info: the dictionary rejects Shakespeare's own temperate/date (see docs/research/verse-dictionary-spike.md), so a miss may be an eye rhyme or a historical pronunciation. Only a certain non-rhyme warns. Why it matters at all: in one small rating study (Obermeier et al., 17 listeners, German stanzas heard aloud) rhymed stanzas were liked more; it compared rhyme with none, so it supports no threshold. A draft may declare its own scheme for words written to an existing tune (frontmatter scheme: xaxa, or a map by section), applied per stanza; that is the author's requirement, not a convention of the form, so it replaces the form's scheme for the check and the same severities apply, with x lines never pairing. A stanza whose line count differs from the declared scheme is skipped here when a declared syllable pattern covers it (the syllables rule speaks), and reported once otherwise. The rule is a no-op for a form without a scheme unless the draft declares one, which is why it now lists every verse form.

conflicts.note: The same end words serve rhyme and meter; swapping a word to mend a rhyme can move a stress. Fix the rhyme first, then re-read the meter.

rules.statement: Each line fits the syllable pattern: the haiku's 5, 7, 5 (soft, info), or one the draft declares in its frontmatter for a tune or hymn meter such as 8.6.8.6 (the author's own requirement, warn).
rules.rationale: poets.org says a traditional Japanese haiku is three lines in a 5/7/5 syllable count, and also that "many of its regular traits—including its famous syllabic pattern—have been routinely broken". Sonnet or Not, Bot says English haiku "often" use 5, 7 and 5 and that haiku can mean concise poems of any line count. So a miss against the haiku pattern is info, never higher. Counts come from CMUdict (US English); a line whose words have more than one count passes when the target falls inside the range. A draft may also declare its own pattern (frontmatter syllables: 8.6.8.6, or a map by section), per stanza and repeated for every stanza; that is the author's requirement for words set to an existing tune, not a convention of the form, so it overrides the form's pattern, a miss is a warning, and a stanza with a different number of lines is reported once. Lines in sections with no declared pattern are not checked. The rule is a no-op for a form without a pattern unless the draft declares one, which is why it now lists every verse form.

conflicts.note: Counting syllables can push a break to where the count falls instead of where the image turns; poets.org says the pattern is routinely broken, so let the break win when it must.

rules.statement: Villanelle refrains repeat verbatim at the required lines (A1 at 1, 6, 12, 18; A2 at 3, 9, 15, 19).
rules.rationale: poets.org gives the notation A1 b A2 / a b A1 / a b A2 / a b A1 / a b A2 / a b A1 A2: the first and third lines are repeated alternately at the end of later stanzas and together in the last two. It also notes that contemporary poets "have loosened the fixed form to allow variations on the refrains", so a changed refrain may be deliberate; the check compares lowercase text with punctuation stripped.

rules.statement: Sestina stanzas rotate the first stanza's six end words in the fixed order, and the envoi holds all six.
rules.rationale: poets.org gives the order ABCDEF, FAEBDC, CFDABE, ECBFAD, DEACFB, BDFECA and an envoi that includes the remaining end words, so all six appear in the last three lines. The sestina has no rhyme scheme ("end-word repetition" stands in for rhyme), so a rhyme check cannot see it and a repetition check is needed; Sonnet or Not, Bot found models struggled with repetition forms. The envoi check requires all six words in the last three lines, not their order (poets.org gives ECA or ACE).

rules.statement: Lines where a polysyllabic word's stress contradicts its slot in the form's meter are listed (advisory).
rules.rationale: poets.org gives the sonnet as iambic pentameter and the limerick as anapestic. Scansion is contested and gradient: a Wikipedia summary (weak evidence) says scansion systems "are so numerous and contradictory" that differences are hard to interpret, and that a regular iambic pentameter line "may have anywhere from 2 to 9 stresses" yet is felt to have 5 beats. So only a polysyllable's dictionary stress against its slot counts; monosyllables never do, a feminine ending is allowed, lines with guessed words are skipped, and nothing is more than info. Regular meter was liked more in one small German rating study (Obermeier et al., 17 listeners; it changed words to change the meter), which supports no tolerance. Which deviations count is this plugin's convention.

conflicts.note: The same end words serve rhyme and meter; swapping a word to fix a stress can break a rhyme. Fix the rhyme first, then re-read the meter.

rules.statement: Words missing from the pronouncing dictionary are listed; verdicts on their lines are weaker.
rules.rationale: A word the dictionary lacks gets a heuristic syllable count, unknown stress and a letters-based rhyme key. PhonologyBench found a vowel-count baseline right on 12.1% of sentences against 90.0% for a human annotator (its gold counts come from a G2P library), and this project's own spike found the heuristic exact on 61 of 72 lines against 71 for the dictionary (small sample, labels written by an AI). So findings on these lines are weaker and meter skips them.

rules.statement: Words with several pronunciations are listed only where the reading matters: an end word whose rhyme depends on it, or a word that decides whether a line fits a declared syllable or meter count.
rules.rationale: The flat CMUdict file has variants but no part of speech (the maintainers list it as undone work), so a heteronym such as "wind" cannot be resolved by the tool and "temperate" can scan as two or three syllables. The check lists them so you can confirm the reading you meant, instead of trusting the first variant.

rules.statement: Free verse of six or more lines where every end word rhymes with another line is flagged as a sameness signal.
rules.rationale: In Porter and Machery's stimuli (ChatGPT 3.5 poems against poems by 10 canonical poets) 89% of the AI poems rhymed at every line against 40% of the human poems. The authors call such heuristics flawed, and all-lines-rhyme was only a "suggestive" predictor (p = 0.016 against a 0.005 threshold); models and readers change. This is a sameness signal for your own review, never an authorship verdict. The six-line minimum is a convention.

rules.statement: A verse line that starts like Markdown (a dash, a number and period, or >) is read as a list item, step or quote, not a line.
rules.rationale: The draft is Markdown, and the parser reads a line starting with a list marker, a number and a period, or > as a list item, step or quote, so the line is still counted but its kind changes. Start the line with a word or escape the marker. A convention of this tool, not a poetics rule.

rules.statement: In a song, a line that is wholly one parenthesised phrase, or a short line giving a tempo (90 bpm) or a time signature (4/4), is read as a direction, not a lyric, and is left out of the measurement.
rules.rationale: A lyric draft is Markdown that mixes sung lines with performance notes such as (hum softly) or Folk, about 90 bpm, 4/4, and the tool must decide which is which. Skipping a wholly parenthesised line, a line of up to twelve words with a bpm figure, or a line of up to six words with a stand-alone time signature is a convention of this tool, not a songwriting rule, and a sung line can look like one. Each skipped line is reported so none vanishes silently; if it is sung, rewrite it without the leading and trailing parentheses or the tempo wording.

rules.statement: A refrain section repeated under the same label matches its first occurrence.
rules.rationale: Musical U says choruses usually repeat melody and lyrics, and the refrain form ends in one or two identical lines; the Berklee syllabus lists "Form: Verse/Refrain". Both are weak evidence (a practitioner article and a course description), and Musical U says none of this "is a rule or a formula". Matching refrains is therefore a convention, and a deliberate change is yours to keep.

rules.statement: Like sections (Verse 1, Verse 2) stay within 2 syllables per line of each other.
rules.rationale: Musical U says verses usually share a melody with new lyrics each time, so lines in like sections have to fit the same tune; a large syllable gap may not fit. That is an inference. The Berklee and Coursera pages list line length and symmetry as course topics without any threshold, and both are course descriptions (weak evidence). The limit of 2 syllables is a convention of this plugin.

rules.statement: Each line ends where it does for a reason: sound, sense, speed or surprise.
rules.rationale: poets.org defines enjambment as "the continuation of a sentence or clause across a poetic line break" and says run-on lines "minimize the difference of sound between verse and prose, while increasing the speed and pacing of a poem". The tool reports only a punctuation proxy (stop, weak, run-on); the source gives no way to detect enjambment mechanically, so whether a break earns its place stays a judgement.

conflicts.note: A syllable count can dictate where a line breaks; poets.org says the haiku pattern is routinely broken, so let the break win when it must.

rules.statement: Stressed syllables meet strong beats when the lyric is set to music.
rules.rationale: Gordon, Magne and Large (16 analysed participants, sung six-syllable sentences at 150 beats per minute) found that the word-versus-pseudoword reaction-time gap was smaller after well-aligned primes than after misaligned ones (misaligned against well-aligned follow-up, p = 0.009; word-versus-pseudoword gaps of about 53 ms after well-aligned primes against 94 ms after misaligned ones, from the table of means), and their abstract says these findings "suggest that alignment of linguistic stress and musical meter in song enhances musical beat tracking and comprehension of lyrics by synchronizing neural activity with strong syllables". It is a lab effect on isochronous sentences, not a threshold for composers. The Berklee and Coursera pages list stress matching as a topic (course descriptions, weak evidence). The tool cannot hear the melody, so this stays a judgement.
